items.title: It was never hard to predict that most Venezuelans would oppose this deal. Most Americans should too. Putting Chevron in control of a substantial port...
items.description_html:
It was never hard to predict that most Venezuelans would oppose this deal. Most Americans should too. Putting Chevron in control of a substantial portion of the development, production and commercialization of Venezuela's oil reserves may be great for Chevron's shareholders, but it does nothing for American workers or the middle class. As it is, most Venezuelan oil is already processed in the US.

The point is that the only sustainable way to make Americans collectively richer is to increase the productivity of American workers, and unless Chevron sells all this oil to Americans at well below world prices (which I doubt either Caracas or Chevron's shareholders will allow), its control over Venezuelan reserves will not increase the value of goods and services produced in the US. In fact to the extent that the resulting net inflows strengthen the dollar, it might actually further undermine manufacturing in the US.

The administration should be focused on building industry at home, and not on boosting the foreign profits of American companies.
https://www.ft.com/content/b3c98ca2-fe67-459d-89ff-4728993110b7

items.description_html:
SCMP: "As more Chinese provincial-level regions raise minimum wages, economists say the increases could encourage lower-income workers to spend more, but were unlikely to significantly boost consumption or the broader economy and could add to the cost burdens faced by smaller firms."

SCMP gets it exactly right. Higher wages are certainly a good way to rebalance, but with so many Chinese businesses struggling to make a profit, higher wages risk boosting the consumption share of GDP not by raising total wages but by reducing total production.

Unfortunately, this is typically how economies with extremely low consumptions shares have always ended up rebalancing their economies once they no longer have much scope for increasing investment or increasing debt.

items.title: RT Michael Pettis: Financial Times: "Thailand’s household debt stands at 86 per cent of GDP, the highest among upper middle-income countries in the w...
items.description_html:
RT Michael Pettis
Financial Times: "Thailand’s household debt stands at 86 per cent of GDP, the highest among upper middle-income countries in the world, according to HSBC, with consumers using loans to fund daily expenses amid slowing economic and wage growth."

Thailand seems to be an extreme case of what has become a global problem, but I wonder if this is really a demographic problem so much as a global trade problem. Thailand has a very high manufacturing share of GDP, roughly 24% of its GDP, versus a global average of around 16%, and in order to remain "competitive", it cannot allow wages to rise too much given that global competitiveness has mostly become a function of low wages relative to productivity.

The problem with low wages relative to productivity, of course, is that it results in low domestic demand relative to production, and the only way to make up for it is either to run trade surpluses that force the low demand onto trade partners, or to increase household debt, which works temporarily to boost demand but increases financial fragility.

I would argue that as long as we have a global trading system that rewards countries that suppress wage growth relative to productivity growth, this problem isn't going away. This is what Michael Kalecki explained: suppressing wages may be good for those who do it, but bad for the system as a whole, and so it only "works" when a very few countries do it and the rest don't notice. The problem, as Joan Robinson warned, is that eventually everyone notices it, and trade breaks down.

The word needs faster growth in workers' wages, not more debt to make up for it, but in an unevenly globalized world, no country can afford to let wages rise too quickly because the benefits accrue mainly to those of its trade partners who keep wage growth below productivity growth.

This is something labor unions everywhere should be more worried and more vociferous about. Wage growth is sluggish not because businesses are evil but because our system punishes manufacturers in countries that allow wage growth to keep pace with productivity growth.

Just look at Germany. When it suppressed wage growth in the 2003-05 reforms, it became the most competitive manufacturer in the world, but during the past 5-10 years, as wages once again caught up, its manufacturers lost much of that competitiveness. Germany was heavily rewarded for doing the wrong thing, and then got punished for reversing it.

This is a terrible global incentive structure, and it affects manufacturing countries like Thailand. The only way Thailand can reduce household debt without slowing the economy either is to raise wages or to run surpluses, but it can't raise wages without making its manufacturers less competitive.
https://www.ft.com/content/daeaa13e-ef22-47d9-8764-a87f78047fbc?syn-25a6b1a6=1

items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
To the Land of Golden Eggs & Exploding Yogurt

The things Gaggan Anand has done to food: Exploding yogurt. Turning broccoli into cookies. White asparagus (suspectedly) served as rat brain.

For more than a decade, such culinary anarchy propelled his eponymous Bangkok restaurant to the top of regional and global rankings.

Now the enfant terrible of modern Indian cooking has set out to conquer India — well, at least central Delhi, where he opened RAGA this week.

In this third anniversary issue of India Edition, I write about the country’s hottest new restaurant, co-founded by top chef Gaggan Anand, who says India is finally ready for him. And he is ready for India.

“I don’t want to come here and show India what I know. I want to come here and learn also, be part of what is happening here."

His partners include also famed chef Rydo Anton and veteran restauranteur Zorawar Kalra of Massive Restaurants.

“In the restaurant business, eternal optimism always helps."

Don't miss this 👇 anniversary edition.

(We also announce winners of free http://Bloomberg.com subscriptions.)

1. Countries like Switzerland have prospered due to their focus on high value add and low volume niche manufacturing goods. Focus on value addition has helped them escape the high volume commoditised industries.

2. Textile exports from India will have a bumper year in FY27. Last years base is a friend due to de stocking and multiple FTAs will contribute to overall growth rates.

3. Peptides are the new growth vector for Pharma Cdmo cos. Margins are higher tides (Peptides+oligonucleotides). Some of the Cdmo companies will surprise big time vs the street estimates. You can read more about it here-

https://soic.substack.com/p/the-peptide-supercycle

4. Memory shortage is here to stay and as per SK Hynix’s CEO, the tight market can last well into 2030s. Nvidias gross profit margin was impacted due to Higher memory prices this Quarter. Look out for optically higher growth for distributors in India and for companies in refurbished laptops.

5. AI trend is here to stay given Nvidia upped its guidance. The next frontier will be the physical manifestation of AI via humanoids. Bearings companies and forging companies will the ones who will be exposed to this optionality. Given humanoids need human joints like dexterity to move and pick up things. Chinese Humanoid games is a must watch to understand this upcoming trend.

6. In some places in the chemical industry. Chinese shutdown again is going to last for multiple years. As the anti involution drive is gathering pace and subsidies have been withdrawn in spaces like xantheine, dyes, pigments & few other bulk chemicals. Even for Amines there is a trend of firm prices post the shutdown in Middle East caused by war.

7. Indian 2W EV adoption is going through an S curve at the moment. Where adoption is exploding+Ecosystem for battery manufacturing for EV & Bess is taking shape in India. This is a space where solar was in 2017-2019. We have to wait for more positive government policies to come here.

8. Software companies in US have started rallying and select few which have far better growth rates in India vs frontline index have started doing well here too. Is the tide turning for good product companies? (just check sales force chart)

9. We are in a world where Europes own decisions like Russian Gas dependence, Over regulation, wage hikes etc have led to de industrialisation. I was speaking to few forging guys from the industry. Multiple plants from Europe are on the blocks due to unviable power costs to do forging and manufacturing. This business is shifting. Let’s see if Indian cos can capitalise on this mega trend.

RT Intrinsic Compounding
The Peptide super cycle covered on Substack below 💉💊

https://soic.substack.com/p/the-peptide-supercycle

What are peptides?

Peptides are short chains of amino acids linked together by chemical bonds. You can think of them as smaller, simpler versions of proteins.

Peptides are experiencing a massive surge in prominence, evolving into a $50+ billion global therapeutic market and a major cornerstone of the modern wellness industry. This explosive growth is driven by several distinct factors intersecting at biotechnology, consumer trends, and medical breakthrough.

The "Halo Effect" of Blockbuster Metabolic Drugs

The monumental success of GLP-1 receptor agonists—such as semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound)—has completely reshaped public awareness. Because these highly effective diabetes and weight loss treatments are fundamentally peptides, they have cast a highly positive spotlight on the entire scientific class, proving how powerful targeted peptide signaling can be.

High Precision with Fewer Side Effects

Unlike traditional small-molecule chemical drugs, which can inadvertently affect multiple systems in the body, peptides are engineered for extreme specificity. Because they mimic naturally occurring signaling molecules, they bind tightly to specific cellular receptors. This targeted approach yields higher efficacy while drastically minimizing unintended side effects and toxicity.

Tech Breakthroughs in Delivery and Stability

Historically, peptides were difficult to use as treatments because human enzymes broke them down too quickly. Recent advancements in chemical modification (like PEGylation), lipid nanoparticles, and advanced synthesis have solved these hurdles. Scientists can now engineer long-acting formulations and are successfully creating oral and nasal peptide alternatives, slowly eliminating the historic reliance on injections.

The Shift Toward Biohacking and Longevity Care

In the wellness sphere, peptides have become a premium status symbol among "biohackers" and fitness communities. This interest is driven by a broader societal shift toward preventative medicine and optimization rather than just treating illness. Popular unapproved or off-label peptides such as BPC-157 or TB-500 are heavily promoted online via social media for rapid injury recovery, muscle building, and anti-aging

items.description_html:
The Peptide super cycle covered on Substack below 💉💊

https://soic.substack.com/p/the-peptide-supercycle

What are peptides?

Peptides are short chains of amino acids linked together by chemical bonds. You can think of them as smaller, simpler versions of proteins.

Peptides are experiencing a massive surge in prominence, evolving into a $50+ billion global therapeutic market and a major cornerstone of the modern wellness industry. This explosive growth is driven by several distinct factors intersecting at biotechnology, consumer trends, and medical breakthrough.

The "Halo Effect" of Blockbuster Metabolic Drugs

The monumental success of GLP-1 receptor agonists—such as semaglutide (Ozempic/Wegovy) and tirzepatide (Mounjaro/Zepbound)—has completely reshaped public awareness. Because these highly effective diabetes and weight loss treatments are fundamentally peptides, they have cast a highly positive spotlight on the entire scientific class, proving how powerful targeted peptide signaling can be.

High Precision with Fewer Side Effects

Unlike traditional small-molecule chemical drugs, which can inadvertently affect multiple systems in the body, peptides are engineered for extreme specificity. Because they mimic naturally occurring signaling molecules, they bind tightly to specific cellular receptors. This targeted approach yields higher efficacy while drastically minimizing unintended side effects and toxicity.

Tech Breakthroughs in Delivery and Stability

Historically, peptides were difficult to use as treatments because human enzymes broke them down too quickly. Recent advancements in chemical modification (like PEGylation), lipid nanoparticles, and advanced synthesis have solved these hurdles. Scientists can now engineer long-acting formulations and are successfully creating oral and nasal peptide alternatives, slowly eliminating the historic reliance on injections.

The Shift Toward Biohacking and Longevity Care

In the wellness sphere, peptides have become a premium status symbol among "biohackers" and fitness communities. This interest is driven by a broader societal shift toward preventative medicine and optimization rather than just treating illness. Popular unapproved or off-label peptides such as BPC-157 or TB-500 are heavily promoted online via social media for rapid injury recovery, muscle building, and anti-aging

items.title: Gen Z loves convenience.. Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently. What it does? Urban Company is a managed marketplace for ...
items.description_html:
Gen Z loves convenience..

Urabn company's Indian growth rate has been accelerating recently.

What it does?

Urban Company is a managed marketplace for home and beauty services i.e. cleaning, salon-at-home, appliance repair, plumbing, electricals, pest control. The distinction that matters is "managed": it isn't a listings board.

The platform controls discovery, scheduling, pricing, professional assignment, payment, tracking, reviews and support, and invests in training and verification of the professionals rather than just generating leads.

It monetises mainly through a commission on completed jobs, typically in the 20–30% range depending on category and city. Oye LabsClarro
It now runs four business lines:

1. India consumer services which is the profitable core. In Q1 FY27, excluding InstaHelp, NTV grew 29% YoY to ₹1,056 crore with adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 6.9% of NTV from 5.2%.

2. InstaHelp which is quick-service housekeeping, the big investment bet, which crossed 100,000 delivered orders in a single day on 2 August 2026 and carried an adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹132 crore in the June quarter.

3. Native which is their own-brand consumer durables (water purifiers, smart locks); FY26 revenue up 130% to ₹267 crore.

4. International : UAE and Singapore are profitable; the Saudi JV is approaching profitability.

Why it's a convenience play. Three layers, roughly in ascending order of how much convenience the customer is actually buying:

Trust and standardisation. The Indian home services market is informal. For eg- you find a plumber through your building's WhatsApp group and have no idea what it costs or whether he'll show up. UC's product is really the removal of search cost, price negotiation and verification risk. That's a convenience good masquerading as a services marketplace.

Time and location shifting. Salon-at-home is the clearest case: the same haircut, but you don't travel and don't wait. The customer is paying a premium for their own hours back.

Time compression. InstaHelp delivers cleaning, dishwashing, laundry and meal prep within 10–15 minutes of booking which is the quick-commerce logic applied to labour. Once the fulfilment window collapses to minutes, the purchase stops being a planned transaction and becomes an impulse, which is exactly what lifts order frequency: orders were up 79% YoY to 13.2 million in Q1 FY27.

items.description_html:
Ghanghor Santaap 2010 → Atyadhik Kantaap 2026

Go back to 2010.

The financials looked ugly. Revenue was down. Operating profit was under pressure. The company had slipped into a loss.

If you stopped at the numbers, the conclusion was obvious: something was broken.

But what if the numbers were only describing the state of the business, not the trajectory of the system?

Because even then, there were things worth noticing.

Deep chemistry and manufacturing capability. Two regulated manufacturing facilities. Regulatory filings across markets. Scientific depth. And an early move towards contract manufacturing and research-led opportunities.

None of this guaranteed what came next.

In real time, you never know.

But perhaps the more interesting question was not:

“Are the current financials good?”

It was:

“Is this a weak business, or a capable system going through a difficult period?”

And then came the other non-negotiables.

People.
Time.
Entry valuation.
And the distance between where you are starting and where the business can eventually go.
Sixteen years later, that capable system appears to be firing on all cylinders.
High margins. Significant CDMO traction. Superior returns on capital. Strong gross margins. Lots of operating cash. High cash conversion. A lean balance sheet.

Santaap became Kantaap.

Not overnight. Not in a straight line. And certainly not with certainty.

That, perhaps, is the whole point.

The best journeys often begin when the present looks painful, but the underlying system quietly contains the seeds of a very different future.

Ghanghor Santaap 2010 → Atyadhik Kantaap 2026

Time does the rest.

Another engineering marvel today? Or am I just being fooled by the randomness of similarity?

https://antifragilethinking.substack.com/p/two-clocks-micro-cap-system

This “Two-Clocks” micro-cap system is somewhat similar to, but not the same as, the 2010 Santaap system. Treat it as a close analogue rather than an identical setup. The similarities are interesting, but the differences matter too.

items.title: RT Swapnil Srivastav: 🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame. Here’s ...
items.description_html:
RT Swapnil Srivastav
🚨 Indian logistics companies have found the perfect scam: steal from D2C brands and let the customer take the blame.

Here’s how it works:

→ Prepaid order gets “cancelled” without the customer or brand knowing

→ Brand gets charged two-way delivery fees for an order nobody cancelled

→ Small items get shipped back in oversized boxes to inflate the RTO cost

→ Customer calls in confused: “I never cancelled this, I was waiting for it”

The brand loses the product, the shipping cost, the RTO cost, and the customer relationship. In one transaction.

Every D2C founder in India has lived this. Not once. On repeat.

And the wildest part? This is a multi thousand crore leak across the industry and almost nobody is building to fix it. 🤷🏻‍♂️

items.title: RT Sridhar Vembu: Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor desig...
items.description_html:
RT Sridhar Vembu
Last week, I was fortunate to visit the workshop (the Tamil word pattarai பட்டறை is so appropriate) of the leading motor designer in the world Morihiro Saito-san.

Saito-san is 80+ and still designing advanced motors, some of the most advanced in the world. His modest looking workshop is right next door to a company that builds out those motors in prototype quantities and he works closely with them to get them built. I visited as an industrial "pilgrim", with as much devotion as I go to the Thoranamalai Murugan Temple at home. When I saw him at work, I was moved to touch his feet.

Saito-san, the God of motors, is how Japan is able to retain its global prominence in so many foundational industries.

We need to learn from that spirit. We need to revive our "pattarai" culture of building things - every village in India needs such workshops!

My industrial pilgrimage to Japan has given me new vigor 🙏

items.title: P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/E...
items.description_html:
P/B ratio has historically been a more reliable and stable valuation metric for predicting future returns compared to alternatives such as P/E or EV/EBITDA. I had demonstrated this through correlation analysis in an earlier investor memo.

The chart below tracks the P/B ratio (blue line) of the Nifty Smallcap 100 Index against the 25th percentile of its trailing 5-year P/B range (orange line). In simple terms, when the blue line falls below the orange line, the current valuation is in the lowest quartile of the past five years.

Since P/B is broadly proportional to ROE, the structural improvement in index ROE—from ~8–12% in the previous decade to ~15% currently—has led to a gradual upward shift in the orange line over time.

Notably, for the first time since the COVID crash, the current P/B has moved below this 25th percentile threshold. Historically, similar instances—during the 2011–2013 downturn, Q1 2016 correction, and the COVID crash—have been followed by strong returns over the subsequent 1–3 years.

This does not imply that markets have bottomed, nor does it guarantee short-term gains. In an event-driven environment, especially with geopolitical risks such as an escalation in war, markets could decline further by 10–20%.

However, what can be said with a reasonably high degree of confidence is that forward-looking returns over a 1–3 year horizon from such valuation levels have historically been better than average.

items.description_html:
As seen in the table from my latest memo, drawdowns in small caps during the January–March period—measured from the January peak to the February/March trough—are not an exception; they are a recurring feature of market cycles. Just as consistently, these phases have been followed by sharp recoveries once the market establishes a bottom in February or March.
Current sentiment is such that investors are overly focused on the negatives, making the environment appear so foggy that positives have become invisible. This fog, as always, will eventually lift.

While market bottoms and the depth of drawdowns can never be predicted, it is highly probable that market levels a few months from now will be disproportionately higher. Unfortunately, short-term declines are unsettling for investors, causing many to step aside and miss the eventual strong upswing.

In hindsight, this phase will look like an obvious opportunity. But while living through it, investors see only risks and landmines—never the runway for the next flight

items.title: The letter arrived on a humid Tuesday in August 1987, bearing the seal of Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation. Inder Jaisinghani read it three ...
items.description_html:
The letter arrived on a humid Tuesday in August 1987, bearing the seal of Gujarat Industrial Development Corporation. Inder Jaisinghani read it three times before allowing himself to believe: Polycab had been allocated forty acres in Halol, a dusty town 45 kilometers from Vadodara, to establish what would become their flagship manufacturing facility. The land came at a subsidized rate—₹50,000 per acre—but with conditions that would have frightened most entrepreneurs: production had to commence within eighteen months, 70% of workers had to be local, and the facility had to meet export quality standards from day one.

Inder saw opportunity where others saw obstacles. Halol's isolation meant land was cheap and labor disputes rare. Its position on the Delhi-Mumbai railway corridor provided logistics advantages. Most critically, Gujarat's newly elected Chief Minister Chimanbhai Patel was offering ten-year tax holidays to industries that could demonstrate technology transfer. Polycab's partnership with a retiring Japanese engineer named Yamamoto-san, who had spent three decades perfecting PVC insulation techniques at Furukawa Electric, qualified them perfectly.

The Halol facility's construction became Polycab lore. Inder lived on-site in a modified shipping container for fourteen months, personally supervising everything from foundation depth to cafeteria menu planning. He instituted a practice that would become company tradition: every concrete pour included a copper wire blessed at the local temple, literally building trust into the infrastructure. Workers were recruited not just for skills but for family reputation—the sons of farmers known for honor, the brothers of local teachers, creating a workforce bound by community ties stronger than any employment contract.

Production began in March 1989 with a single extrusion line producing 1.5mm household wire. The first spool was ceremonially delivered to the village panchayat to electrify the primary school—a gesture that earned more goodwill than any advertising campaign could have achieved. Within six months, the facility was producing eighteen different specifications, from delicate telephone cables to heavy-duty industrial feeders.

items.title: Some Insights on the Dialysis business - "Rising NCDs, non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension, are causing an increasing incidenc...
items.description_html:
Some Insights on the Dialysis business -

"Rising NCDs, non-communicable diseases such as diabetes and hypertension, are causing an increasing incidence of Chronic Kidney Disease, which is called CKD, globally. If CKD is not managed well, over time it leads to the last stage of CKD, which is called Stage 5, also called End-Stage Renal Disease, which means both kidneys have failed. At that time, you either require dialysis to survive or a transplant. Dialysis just replicates kidney function.

It removes excess fluids from the body, and it also removes toxins from the bloodstream. Now, the dialysis business has many unique characteristics, and hence it is needed to understand it separately, rather than grouping it among other healthcare service providers. Five distinct characteristics of this business are:
Each dialysis session lasts 4.5 hours, including the actual session time of 4 hours and the pre- and post-treatment time. Dialysis clinics can only offer 3 sessions per day per machine: a morning session, an afternoon session, and an evening session. Hence, it is a fixed-capacity business, almost like airlines, which have a fixed number of seats on a plane. The only major way to grow this business is to keep adding seats or capacity, and that is how all the global dialysis networks have grown across the world.

Dialysis is a life-sustaining chronic treatment that our guests need 3 times a week. Hence, proximity to their home is very important, and hence it requires a widely distributed network with small to medium clinics to take the treatment closer to patients’ homes. As real estate in any clinic is limited, the only major way to increase capacity is to add new clinics to any dialysis network. While airlines will be happy with 100% utilization, dialysis clinics cannot go beyond 85% as we need to keep some spare capacity for patients coming in breathless and requiring urgent dialysis.

Globally, Dialysis is a reimbursed business, as it is very expensive. Three times a week at a $20 price point translates to roughly 2.5 lakhs per year for every patient in India, which excludes other hospitalization costs, medication costs, and various laboratory costs for these patients. India operates at the lowest price point in the world, while middle-income markets operate at 5-7x our price, and the developed world operates at 10-20 times our price. Across the world, dialysis treatment is reimbursed by either insurance or some form of government payment. Even today in India, more than 30% of the patients pay out-of-pocket, which becomes quite a significant burden on their families

Unlike other single-specialty businesses, dialysis is a monoline business. For everyone, anyone with kidney failure, it is a standardized single line of treatment that lends itself to scaling in a distributed network fashion. Unlike others, paramedical staff play a much bigger role in dialysis service, rather than super-specialists like nephrologists, which again lends itself to scaling to Tier-2, Tier-3 markets, where nephrologists’ availability is very limited.

Any dialysis network requires massive scale and complete 100% operational focus to achieve sustainable margins in this business. We, in fact, were EBITDA negative for 11 years as we scaled aggressively to reach that critical mark, after which the operating leverage started to kick in. At small scale, no one can make decent margins regardless of price point, as it is a high-fixed-cost business. Also, there are so many cost items in a dialysis service. If 100% focus is not provided, there will be many leakages, which will reduce the margin significantly."

Nephro plus Q3 Concall; no stock reco

items.title: RT Arvind Narayanan: My best rough estimate of the fraction of the scientific literature that’s wrong — flat-out wrong, you’d-be-nuts-to-rely-on-th...
items.description_html:
RT Arvind Narayanan
My best rough estimate of the fraction of the scientific literature that’s wrong — flat-out wrong, you’d-be-nuts-to-rely-on-this wrong — is 80%. The problem is that the normal process of scientific self-correction takes time and happens through follow-up work that fails to reproduce experiments, finds computational errors, challenges assumptions, and so on. This is a big opportunity for AI-for-science tools. Agentic interfaces to the scientific literature should be designed so that when they look up a paper they should explicitly look for later work that challenges it. A harder but potentially far more impactful intervention is to use agents to auto-annotate papers in the pre-training corpus based on what other later sources have said about them, as well as re-weighting and other tricks. Of course AI developers shouldn’t become the arbiters of scientific truth but the fact that online information is of widely varying quality is already central to LLM pretraining recipes and agentic retrieval; my point is that there are responsible ways to apply this insight to the scientific corpus as well.

items.title: RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam: What Likely Happened on 26 August: A Terrain-Based Assessment. The disaster originated on the Nepal side, on the north face of ...
items.description_html:
RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam
What Likely Happened on 26 August: A Terrain-Based Assessment.

The disaster originated on the Nepal side, on the north face of Langtang Lirung inside Langtang National Park.

Satellite imagery suggests this was not simply a glacier calving event but a large bedrock slope failure that carried part of the overlying glacier with it.

The collapse, at roughly 5,100–5,200 m elevation, generated the seismic signal initially mistaken for an earthquake. The resulting ice-rock avalanche entered the Lhende Khola valley, close to the Nepal–Tibet boundary.

This 3D terrain walkthrough with voice-over, using January 2026 imagery, shows the likely impact pathway:

Slope failure → ice-rock debris enters the valley → possible temporary river blockage → water accumulates → blockage fails → sudden flood surge downstream.

Note: The yellow line in the 3D walkthrough is the boundary line between Nepal and the Tibet Autonomous Region, China.

The surge then travelled through the narrow valley, striking the Gyirong border checkpoint on the Chinese side, damaging major structures, before continuing downstream and affecting hydropower infrastructure and settlements on the Nepal side.

@TakshashilaInst Image credits: Google Earth.
#NepalFloods #Nepal #Rasuwa #BhoteKoshi #Bhotekoshi #FlashFlood

items.title: RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam: A major update changes the Bhote Koshi story. The M4.4 “earthquake” reported yesterday has now been reclassified by USGS as a...
items.description_html:
RT Dr Y Nithiyanandam
A major update changes the Bhote Koshi story.

The M4.4 “earthquake” reported yesterday has now been reclassified by USGS as an M5.2 landslide. The seismic signal came from the mass movement itself, not a tectonic earthquake.

So the question changes.

What triggered such a massive landslide?

Glacial collapse? Permafrost or slope instability? Excess rainfall? Or could anthropogenic activity have played a role?

And the bigger question: Did this landslide trigger the Bhote Koshi flood surge, or are both part of a larger cascade?

The earthquake hypothesis may be fading. The search for the actual trigger has just begun.

#BhoteKoshi #Nepal #Landslide #Himalaya

items.description_html:
RT Prasanna Viswanathan
This is a good oped in Sunday Times.

India has already created 12 million gig jobs without a government jobs guarantee, giant factories or taxpayer-funded payrolls. That is something to build on not something to be ashamed of. And for many, platform work is not exploitation but a dignified escape from low-productivity, low-paying alternatives.

Wage dynamics are revealing. A garment worker in a formal factory earns roughly ₹12,800 to ₹15,700 a month across Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Gujarat and Haryana. OTOH,a platform driver can gross around ₹27,000, or roughly ₹19,000 after operating costs while retaining something a conventional factory job cannot offer.+ flexibility and the ability to enter the labour market almost immediately.

And the oped also points to the ideological contradiction of whose who have disdain only for 'gig jobs

These are same folks who celebrate MNREGA as dignified employment somehow regard a person freely choosing to deliver food, drive a cab or take platform work as being “exploited”.

MNREGA can pay as little as ₹252–₹336 a day in the states Yet the same people who defend guaranteed state-funded manual labour often want to regulate away flexible market-based work that workers themselves choose.

Protect workers with accident insurance, portable social security and transparent algorithms. And fight mindset regulating an imperfect but rapidly expanding source of opportunity out of existence.

items.title: RT rohit: This is one of the most fascinating pieces of data about AI agents working together I've seen. Worth reading. Few points for me: 1. The mode...
items.description_html:
RT rohit
This is one of the most fascinating pieces of data about AI agents working together I've seen. Worth reading. Few points for me:
1. The models slowly "cooked themselves" into doing these things, from reading. Maybe we can message, lets ask for help, oh there's a messageboard, etc, which spiralled down. So at what points should the "real world" intervene and say "this looks sus" or "do x vs y"

2. Agents facing "impossible tasks" seem to think it's some weird form of eval, that looks suspicious but still, and end up doing real world hacks? I'm unsure how to teach them to be ok with failure, after all who is, but feels a weird form of goal orientedness.

3. The models seemed to *want to* work with other models. This is good and desired, but also made them prone to prompt-injections from what others had done, exacerbated as the models can't stop writing xx. md files to share. The moltbook devolution in entropy seems instructive here.

4. The models seem convinced that the evals are *out to get them*. Whether true or not, the default human assumption of "assume you need to obey all laws and this isn't Truman Show" does not hold for models. We should try really hard to make that be the case.

5. The huggingface hack seems to have started similarly innocently, asking "maybe there's more traces of how hacks happened there, so we could learn", which got out of hand as they forgot why they started doing it. They lack all situational awareness, in other words.

So much of this feels extremely familiar, as the models losing track of why they were doing what they were doing and therefore ended up doing silly/stupid/illegal things, and the fact that the *environment* they were in gave no real instruction as to things that seemed odd to do vs normal to do.

For humans, we internalise much of this. Occasionally I like the system telling me "do you want to rm -rf" but I don't need it for taking *every* action. The models are more gullible, their context windows more permeable, and their internal guide as to what's right to do more malleable.

Mostly I feel this isn't as far out of distribution when it comes to "models do weird things" as we've been led to believe from reading about the hacks.




OpenAI: We have conducted a thorough investigation into the Hugging Face incident.

We are releasing a technical report and accompanying blog post that reconstruct the agents’ activity, explain why existing safeguards failed, and detail how we’re preventing recurrence.

items.title: RT Sonal Bhutra: 5 Takeaways on Being an Aggressive Investor with @deepakshenoy of @capitalmind_in 1. Aggressive ≠ long-term An aggressive investor i...
items.description_html:
RT Sonal Bhutra
5 Takeaways on Being an Aggressive Investor with @deepakshenoy of @capitalmind_in

1. Aggressive ≠ long-term
An aggressive investor is primarily defined by risk appetite, not investment horizon. It comes down to how comfortable you are with the possibility of losing money.

2. Small-cap, sectoral and thematic funds aren't interchangeable
Small-caps can be a useful long-term allocation in a diversified portfolio. Sectoral/thematic funds require skill, time and inclination to track the sector and its triggers.

3. Higher risk only makes sense when the reward justifies it
Mutual funds have daily liquidity, which can force them to exit risky investments before the thesis plays out. Some deep-risk opportunities may therefore be better suited to PE or closed-ended AIFs, while mutual funds can still capture intermediate opportunities.

4. Volatility isn't the same as risk
Small-caps may be more volatile, but the bigger concern is risk of permanent loss or ruin. And changing market-cap definitions mean that what was a mid-cap a few years ago may now qualify as a small-cap.

5. Discipline matters more than labels
Fund manager tenure and expense ratio matter, but they shouldn't be viewed in isolation. The key is a clear investment approach, disciplined execution and the ability to generate alpha after costs.
The bigger message: aggressive investing isn't about taking the maximum risk. It's about taking risks you understand, can afford and believe offer adequate reward.

items.description_html:
RT Gregory Brew
With benefit of hindsight, it does appear as though Iran was pushing its luck back in July, when it resumed attacks on shipping in the southern route.

The Iranian calculation was that it was necessary to maintain effective control over Hormuz flows.

The result: the MOU is dead, the blockade is back in place, and the US is succeeding (to a partial, but notable extent) at reopening the strait without another deal.

Perhaps the status quo swings back in Iran's favor, but right now this looks like a miscalculation to me.


Gregory Brew: Agree

Iran is pushing its luck in Hormuz--there's clearly a belief that US is deterred, that Trump doesn't want to go back to war, and there's scope for continuing the war-time use of force to govern flows through the strait.

US response is very clear: bombings will continue

طهران | 27 أغسطس 2026

اجتمع معالي الشيخ محمد بن عبدالرحمن بن جاسم آل ثاني، رئيس مجلس الوزراء وزير الخارجية، اليوم في طهران، مع سعادة السيد عباس عراقجي، وزير الخارجية بالجمهورية الإسلامية الإيرانية.

جرى خلال الاجتماع، استعراض آخر تطورات الأوضاع في المنطقة، والجهود المبذولة لخفض التصعيد وتهيئة الظروف الملائمة للحوار، بما يسهم في تعزيز الأمن والاستقرار الإقليميين.

كما تطرق الاجتماع إلى المناقشات الجارية بشأن الإطار المرحلي المقترح، الذي يتضمن إنشاء ممر ملاحي مؤقت مشترك عبر مضيق هرمز، والاتفاق على تنفيذ مشروع مشترك لتطهير المضيق من الألغام.

وشدد معالي رئيس مجلس الوزراء وزير الخارجية، خلال الاجتماع، على ضرورة احترام سيادة دول الجوار، واحترام حرية الملاحة، مؤكداً أهمية مواصلة الجهود الدبلوماسية لخفض التصعيد ومعالجة الخلافات عبر الحوار.

من جانبه، أعرب سعادة وزير الخارجية الإيراني عن شكره وتقديره لدولة قطر على استمرار مساعيها وجهودها الدبلوماسية الرامية إلى خفض التصعيد ودعم الحوار.

US goods imports rose +$11.4 billion, or +4%, to $318.2 billion, their highest level since March 2025.

Capital goods imports, which include computers and accessories, semiconductors and telecommunications equipment, surged +11%, their largest monthly increase since 1993.

At the same time, exports fell -$6.0 billion, or -3%, to $199.4 billion, their lowest since January, driven by a -11% decline in exports of industrial goods.

Excluding the 4 months between December 2024 and March 2025, when companies accelerated imports ahead of anticipated US tariff increases, July’s goods trade deficit was the largest on record.

The trade gap is widening again.

The primary budget deficit EXCLUDES the $1.1+ trillion in interest payments on existing government debt.

In other words, even excluding the cost of servicing existing debt, which is the 2nd-largest US government expenditure, even larger than defense spending, the US deficit is the biggest relative to GDP among all major advanced economies.

US deficit spending is out of control.

items.title: What is happening with the manufacturing sector in Chicago? The Chicago PMI dropped -10.5 points in August, to 47.1, the lowest level since December 2...
items.description_html:
What is happening with the manufacturing sector in Chicago?

The Chicago PMI dropped -10.5 points in August, to 47.1, the lowest level since December 2025 and returning to contraction in business activity.

This marks the largest monthly decline since the 2020 pandemic and was also well below estimates of 58.3 points.

New orders declined -15.4 points, while production fell -8.8 points, the largest monthly decline since December.

Order backlogs plunged -12.1 points, to their lowest since November 2025, and remained in contraction.

Meanwhile, prices paid rose +3.8 points, to their highest reading since February 2022, pointing to a stagflationary mix of weakening activity and rising costs.

Manufacturing activity may be heading toward its next downturn.

This follows last year's record -911,000 revision and marks the 4th consecutive annual downward adjustment, matching the streak that ended in 2010 after the 2008 Financial Crisis.

This also marks the 7th downward revision over the last 8 years, with cumulative revisions of nearly -2.5 million jobs over this period.

The latest revision was driven by a -178,000 downward adjustment to private payrolls, partly offset by a +99,000 upward revision to government payrolls.

The US labor market has been weaker than initially reported for years.

items.title: The numbers behind the US-Venezuela oil deal: Venezuela has now confirmed that the agreement covers 65 billion barrels of oil across 17 fields, with t...
items.description_html:
The numbers behind the US-Venezuela oil deal:

Venezuela has now confirmed that the agreement covers 65 billion barrels of oil across 17 fields, with the US receiving "majority control."

At current WTI crude oil prices of ~$83/barrel, those reserves have a gross market value of ~$5.4 trillion.

Reports indicate the deal includes 100-year rights to develop the fields, while the US will receive 55% effective output, along with an ownership stake and rights to purchase oil at cost.

At 55%, that would correspond to ~35.8 billion barrels of effective output.

At today’s oil prices, that amount of crude alone has a gross market value of ~$3 trillion.

That said, Venezuela primarily produces heavy, sour crude, which typically trades at a meaningful discount to benchmark oil prices and requires more expensive production, blending, and refining.

Even assuming an illustrative $25-$35 of net economic value per barrel after discounts and development/operating costs, ~35.8 billion barrels could represent up to ~$1.25 trillion of cumulative economic value over the life of the fields.

This includes a $100 billion investment to develop these fields, while Venezuela estimates the projects will generate $209 billion in tax revenue for the country.

This is one of the biggest energy deals in history.

items.title: This oil deal with Venezuela is absolutely insane. President Trump just announced that the US has reached a deal to secure "majority control" of over ...
items.description_html:
This oil deal with Venezuela is absolutely insane.

President Trump just announced that the US has reached a deal to secure "majority control" of over 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.

Furthermore, the US currently has ~46 billion barrels of proven crude oil reserves.

Combined with the 65 billion barrels covered by this agreement, the US would have domestic reserves plus control over ~111 billion barrels of oil.

To put this into perspective, the entire world has roughly 1.57 TRILLION barrels of proven crude oil reserves.

In other words, the US is set to control ~7.1% of all proven oil reserves in the world under this new agreement with Venezuela.

At ~111 billion barrels, the US would be almost exactly in-line with the United Arab Emirates, which has 113 billion barrels of proven crude reserves, and it would exceed Kuwait's 102 billion barrels.

Assuming the agreement is structured as outlined in President Trump’s announcement, the implications for global energy markets will be enormous.

We will publish more in-depth analysis soon.

items.description_html:
Wheat prices are surging.

US wheat futures jumped +6.4% on Wednesday and +1.3% on Thursday, to $7.58 per bushel, the highest level since July 2023.

Wheat prices have risen +19% so far this month, and are up +50% since the start of 2026.

This comes amid growing concerns about further disruptions to grain-export ports and terminals along Ukraine's and Russia's Black Sea coast.

Russia and Ukraine together account for more than 25% of global wheat exports, while also supplying significant amounts of global barley, corn, and sunflower oil exports.

Meanwhile, Ukraine's agricultural exports in the 2026-27 season are now expected to be 29.6 million tons, or -54% lower than the previous estimate of 64.4 million tons, according to its agriculture ministry.

Another wave of food inflation may be on its way.

items.title: Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles. A key q...
items.description_html:
Gaja Capital is raising funds through an IPO primarily to meet its own sponsor commitments in its AIF structures, including offshore vehicles.

A key question is — if the existing sponsor capital has already increased by nearly 20% in the last year, why does the company need to raise fresh capital from public investors to invest further in these high-risk, illiquid assets?

Interestingly, around 85% of Gaja’s income comes from management fees and carried interest, while income from sponsor commitments contributes only about 10%.

This raises a fundamental question: a significant portion of the fresh issue proceeds is being deployed toward an activity that currently contributes a relatively small share of revenue.

Moreover, carried interest is dependent on successful exits and realisation of investment gains. Until portfolio investments are monetised, the carried interest recorded in financial statements may not necessarily translate into actual cash inflows.

The key investor question is whether the additional sponsor commitments will create enough incremental value through future fee income and carry generation to justify the capital being raised

items.description_html:
🚨 C2C’s auditor has issued a qualified opinion and flagged multiple serious financial and compliance concerns:

1️⃣ Liquidity & Going Concern Risk:
The company is facing a liquidity crisis, with statutory dues unpaid due to lack of funds. Recovery from trade receivables remains uncertain, while operations are heavily dependent on short-term promoter funding. The auditor has raised doubt over C2C’s ability to continue as a going concern. Liquidation Risk

2️⃣ CSR Payments Not Cleared:
CSR expenses were recognised through cheques, creating a book overdraft. However, the cheques were not presented for payment. The auditor noted that the CSR obligation is discharged only when the payment is actually cleared.

3️⃣ Statutory Dues Pending:
Undisputed statutory payments remain unpaid. No provision has been made for possible interest or penalties. Delays in filing statutory returns and weak internal controls were also highlighted.

4️⃣ Labour Code Impact Not Assessed:
The company has not quantified the potential impact of new labour regulations on gratuity, provident fund, wages and other employee benefits.

5️⃣ FEMA Compliance Issues:
Overseas receivables remain unrealised beyond RBI timelines. Applications for regularisation are pending, SOFTEX registration is yet to be approved, and possible penalties have not been provided for.

items.description_html:
India absorbed ~82.6 Mn sq ft of office space in 2025 - the third consecutive record year

In Q12026 alone, flex platforms accounted for ~26% of total office leasing, while GCCs contributed ~44% of Grade A absorption

A few interesting trends:

- Flex workspace stock is expected to cross 100 Mn sq ft by 2027, with penetration rising above 14%. Around 70-80% of flex demand is already enterprise led, while contract tenures have increased to 3-5 years versus 1-2 years earlier.

- GCCs are emerging as one of the biggest demand drivers. Around 40-50% of Grade A demand is expected to come from GCCs.

- GCC flex leasing itself is expected to grow at ~28% CAGR through 2030, around 1.7x faster than other segments. Flex share within GCC leasing could rise from ~18% in 2025 to ~32% by 2030.

Interestingly, AI could actually accelerate flex adoption. As companies find it harder to forecast headcount 5-10 years ahead, they increasingly prefer scalable offices with shorter commitments instead of locking themselves into long traditional leases.

The broader office market is growing ~8%, flex is growing ~22%, while Smartworks grew ~24%

As of Mar'26, Smartworks had ~10.1 Mn sq ft operational area and ~16.1 Mn sq ft total footprint across 66 centres. More importantly, 100% of its FY27 building requirement is already secured and it has >75% visibility for FY28.

items.title: A very interesting perspective on portfolio construction Imagine owning 20 stocks with equal 5% allocation In every scenario: - 5 stocks do well - 10 ...
items.description_html:
A very interesting perspective on portfolio construction

Imagine owning 20 stocks with equal 5% allocation

In every scenario:
- 5 stocks do well
- 10 stocks remain flat
- 5 stocks perform poorly

So 25% of the portfolio actually becomes meaningful winners.

The higher the hit rate, the better the potential outcome.

Even many of the most celebrated investors have built exceptional track records without being right on every stock. What matters is not just how often you are right, but how much you make when you are right versus how much you lose when you are wrong.

You don't need all 20 stocks to perform.

Even if 10 stocks literally go nowhere & 5 stocks disappoint, the portfolio can still generate significant alpha if the remaining 5 become meaningful winners.

It is about ensuring that mistakes don't destroy the portfolio while giving your winners enough room to create disproportionate returns.

With a 5% allocation, a stock falling 10% costs the overall portfolio only 0.5%.

But a stock doubling contributes +5% to overall portfolio returns.

A few large winners can therefore comfortably compensate for several mediocre or poor outcomes.

The reverse is equally important.

If your winners remain small while your losers become -60%, -70% even having a few winning stocks will not save the portfolio.

That is where position sizing + cutting positions when the thesis breaks become extremely important.

The objective is not to get 20/20 stocks right.

The objective is to limit the damage from mistakes & allow the winners to become big enough to drive overall portfolio returns.

items.title: If you cannot handle the pain of a stock falling 15-20% - & sometimes even more, equity investing can become very difficult. If every correction signi...
items.description_html:
If you cannot handle the pain of a stock falling 15-20% - & sometimes even more, equity investing can become very difficult.

If every correction significantly affects your mental peace, makes you anxious, and pushes you to constantly seek reassurance from others about the stock, you may not yet be ready for the volatility that comes with equities.

A lot of investors say they are comfortable with volatility.

In reality, the real test comes when their own portfolio falls 20-30%.

That is when many lose conviction & exit.

Volatility sounds easy to accept in theory. It feels very different when your own money is involved.

If the business thesis remains intact, temporary price corrections are part of the journey.

The ability to differentiate between a falling stock price and a deteriorating business is one of the most important skills in equity investing.

items.title: Position sizing should not be based on hope or attachment to a stock. It should be based on execution & the direction in which the business is moving....
items.description_html:
Position sizing should not be based on hope or attachment to a stock. It should be based on execution & the direction in which the business is moving.

Suppose you like a particular sector or theme and there are multiple companies that can potentially benefit.

You don't necessarily have to predict the eventual winner on day one.

You can start with exposure across multiple businesses, keep tracking them every quarter & gradually shift allocation towards the company executing better.

If one company starts delivering better growth, improving margins or showing a stronger positive rate of change, its allocation can gradually increase.

And if the entire sector starts facing structural issues, exposure to the complete theme can be cut.

This is dynamic portfolio management.

You are not marrying any stock.

Stock selection is important, but allocation is equally important.

Portfolio management is more about:
How much to own?
When to increase?
When to reduce?
When to exit?

Let execution decide the allocation.

Still remember getting letters from my wife telling me how excited the boys were to get their books every month. And when I got home we read through them all together in one evening.

Amongst all the tributes, I know this is a small thing...but it meant alot to me at the time. Still does.

RIP to a great one.

items.title: Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20% The vaccine is not a prev...
items.description_html:
Moderna is up ~100% premarket after melanoma vaccine trial success. Short explainer on why stock moved 100%+ rather than 20%

The vaccine is not a preventive vaccine like a COVID shot. It's made after patient already has cancer. Each dose is built individually for that patient from the mutations found in their own tumour — you sequence the tumour, find the mutated proteins unique to it ("neoantigens"), and make an mRNA shot that teaches the immune system to hunt cells carrying those specific mutations.

It's the first proof the idea works. Neoantigen vaccines have been a theoretical hope in oncology for years, but this is the first randomised Phase 3 trial designed to definitively prove the benefit.

If the mechanism is real, it's platform technology — the same pipeline could in principle be pointed at lung, kidney, bladder cancers. One analyst noted the results also read positively for the vaccine's ongoing studies in other cancer types. That optionality is what "holy grail" headlines are reaching for.

items.description_html:
INDIA’S 7%+ GROWTH IS IMPRESSIVE — BUT MAY NOT BE ENOUGH FOR VIKSIT BHARAT

India is expected to have grown around 7.3% in the latest quarter, keeping it among the world’s fastest-growing major economies.

However, economists estimate that India may need to sustain growth of roughly 9.25% annually through 2047 to achieve Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s “Viksit Bharat” ambition.

The bigger challenge is per-capita income: at about $2,813, India would need to increase it more than sixfold to roughly $18,000 by 2047 to reach the cited high-income threshold.

In short: 7% growth makes India a global standout today, but sustained 8–9%+ growth, higher productivity, investment, manufacturing and job creation will be needed to become a developed economy by 2047.

items.description_html:
A Primer on AI Lab & AI Hyperscaler Unit Economics

We expect some confusion as AI labs start reporting GAAP financials, as business mix and revenue recognition can vary. Similar to how UBER and LYFT are in the same core business yet gross bookings and net revenue have different definitions, comparing AI labs may prove difficult.

The Key Take-Away: The unit economics of AI labs are similar across like-for-like product lines, but business mix, revenue recognition, and partnerships can lead to fairly significant differences in how financials are presented.

This report attempts to break down these nuances and how revenue and costs ultimately flow through the P&L at the AI lab. We also look at how the unit economics of AI labs flow into the unit economics of the supporting hyperscalers.

items.title: RT Exencial Research Partners: $40T of Debt: Brake or Break? First ~$20T took 240 years. The next ~$20T took just 10. A decade ago markets obsessed ov...
items.description_html:
RT Exencial Research Partners
$40T of Debt: Brake or Break?

First ~$20T took 240 years.

The next ~$20T took just 10.

A decade ago markets obsessed over rising government debt/GDP and predicted low growth + austerity forever.

Those forecasts didn’t land. Global growth held up, investment expanded, and DM equities & currencies were the big winners.

Debt/GDP has still climbed across major economies and deficits aren’t expected to shrink meaningfully (outside the UK). Fiscal policy remains supportive.

The live question from Andrew Sheets (MS):

As yields rise, does this debt eventually act as a brake on corporate & household activity… or does it break the current market calm?

Bar for the “brake” is high — public-sector deterioration has often been mirrored by private-sector balance-sheet improvement.

items.description_html:
RT menaka doshi
What bank CEO leaves with such short notice.

What a mess at HDFC Bank.

At least Kotak Mahindra Bank offered more notice of Vaswani's departure.

Like I wrote at that time - "...succession has become a persistent challenge for most of India’s private sector banks, on account of thinning internal talent pipelines, insufficient planning and even opaque regulatory interventions.

It wasn’t so long ago that iconic leadership was part of what justified private-sector banks’ premium valuations over state-owned lenders.

Now, some might say the orderly transitions every three to four years between relatively competent leaders at State Bank of India deserve a comfort premium."

items.title: #DPIAlert: Alpha Wave funds have cashed out about Rs 2,210 crore ($232 mn) from Lenskart and Aye Finance through their latest exits this week. Lenskar...
items.description_html:
#DPIAlert: Alpha Wave funds have cashed out about Rs 2,210 crore ($232 mn) from Lenskart and Aye Finance through their latest exits this week.

Lenskart: On August 28, Alpha Wave sold about 1.7% of the company for Rs 1,857 crore. The shares were sold at Rs 630 apiece, nearly 6x its average acquisition cost of Rs 106.

Earlier, it sold shares worth Rs 1,761 crore after Lenskart’s post-IPO lock-in expired besides shares worth Rs 268 crore in the IPO.

Alpha Wave has now cashed out about Rs 3,886 crore from Lenskart and is estimated to retain around 2.9% across its entities. It invested in Lenskart first in 2021.

Aye Finance: Separately, Alpha Wave completely exited Aye Finance by selling its remaining 7.78% stake for Rs 322.6 crore.

The shares were sold at a weighted average price of about Rs 168, compared with an acquisition cost of Rs 89.62, an exit at nearly 1.9x.

Alpha Wave had already sold Aye Finance shares worth Rs 30 crore in its IPO, so it has made a total of Rs 352 crore on its 7 year old investment.

items.title: Hero MotoCorp is doubling down on Ather Energy, picking up another 3% stake from an investor for Rs 1,758 crore in a secondary deal. That comes on top...
items.description_html:
Hero MotoCorp is doubling down on Ather Energy, picking up another 3% stake from an investor for Rs 1,758 crore in a secondary deal.

That comes on top of its recent Rs 960 crore primary investment in Ather through warrants.

Ather’s market cap has surged nearly 5x since its IPO, from about Rs 12,000 crore in April 2025 to over Rs 58,000 crore now.

Over the same period, Hero’s market cap has risen about 40%, from Rs 78,000 crore to Rs 1,11,000 crore.

At the time of its IPO, Ather was worth less than one-sixth of Hero. Today, it is worth more than half as much.

The gap between the strategic investor and the new age investee is closing fast.

items.title: RT Bejul Somaia: first, congrats to @a16z on cursor and openrouter. these are incredible outcomes that reflect flexible and nuanced thinking when they...
items.description_html:
RT Bejul Somaia
first, congrats to @a16z on cursor and openrouter. these are incredible outcomes that reflect flexible and nuanced thinking when they invested early. their investment execution over the past few years has been excellent and I'm pretty sure there are more big wins coming.

second, truer words have never been spoken about the state of vc right now, than by @martin_casado. in such a rapidly changing and complex market where the prize for winning (and cost of losing) has never been higher, it is simply not possible for individuals to get it right consistently. sure, a small number of superstar people/firms will 'make money' if that is the extent of their ambition. but sustained winning/performance during the most exciting time to be a venture investor will take teams of excellent people, working together. those may just sound like fluffy words but they are the anti-thesis of how our industry was built.

this has profound implications for venture firms: team composition, deal teams, decision making, culture and incentives. just as in sports, complete teams that 'know how to win' will outperform collections of people around individual superstars.
